prize_parts.citation: for methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, which transformed empirical industrial organization and the analysis of market power and welfare

statement.case_for: My configuration has not changed: B001 as a single part, credited to Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn, with a citation tied to demand estimation with endogenous prices and market power. What round 1 changed is how I state the unit of the prize and the limits of my confidence. On merit, the case is that BLP-type estimation answered a concrete measurement problem, recovering substitution patterns and markups from market data when prices are endogenous. It changed what economists can say about market power and welfare, and it moved well beyond industrial organisation. On maturity, I weight the thirty years of repeated re-implementation on different data sets, with different algorithms and instruments, because that is the nearest thing this literature has to a many-analyst replication. Numerical fragility and weak identification were found in that process and were then largely fixed with better algorithms and diagnostics. The result is a method whose failure modes are known, not one that has yet to be tested. On exact credit, I would keep the citation at the method level, as Hassler and Friberg argue. The dynamic-industry and production-function strands then stay as context and are not claimed by the citation. That avoids crediting work with co-authors outside the credited names. It also keeps the unit of the prize identifiable. For the chair's toolkit-versus-discovery question, my criterion is whether the contribution created new counterfactual statements that earlier approaches could not support and whether it changed practice. B001 meets both on the evidence already cited. I treat that as a judgement about the work and not as an inference from first-place counts.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that this honours a measurement toolkit, and the Committee may reasonably weigh that below a substantive discovery. The method-level citation also leaves out Bresnahan, whose role in the new empirical IO programme is large. It also leaves out Reiss, Benkard and Levin, and it claims only part of Pakes's contribution. Applied BLP results can be sensitive to numerical implementation (local optima in the nonlinear search), to instrument choice and to functional form. These sensitivities can change elasticities and so predicted merger price effects in individual applications. The sensitivities are documented but I have not verified how often they reverse a policy conclusion, and my claim that they are largely addressed rests on background knowledge. Taking my own replication-oriented criterion seriously, this is the point where the case for B001 is least checked.

responses.point: Krusell names Pakes, Berry and Bresnahan for B001. He argues that the accomplishment to reward is the wider lineage of estimating demand and supply together to measure market power, production-function methods and dynamic industry models. On this view Levinsohn's role is mostly captured in a single paper, and a Levinsohn version would not be a scientific error.
responses.response: I accept that the choice between us is a choice between framings and not a difference in quality. His answer to the unit-of-the-prize question is more coherent than I allowed in round 1. If the citation is programme-level, Bresnahan belongs in it and Levinsohn's claim weakens. My remaining concern is that the programme-level lineage he describes is already carried largely by Pakes through the production-function and dynamic-game work. A programme-level citation would then credit people for work that sits partly outside the credited names, and it would make the claims harder to check. I therefore keep the method-level citation and Levinsohn. I would support a Pakes, Berry, Bresnahan version, with the citation reworded so that it does not describe the 1995 paper's contribution as Bresnahan's, if that is the version the Committee can assemble. I would not drop Pakes or Berry under either framing.

responses.point: Hassler keeps B001 first with the BLP trio. He argues for defining the unit narrowly as demand and competition estimation in differentiated-product markets plus the dynamic-industry framework. He warns that widening it to production-function estimation or entry models would blur the unit and reopen attribution, and that B002 should be a clean Kiyotaki-Moore pair.
responses.response: I agree with the warning and have drawn the citation accordingly. I dropped the dynamic-industry wording from my citation, and my round 1 citation had left it out in any case. Ericson-Pakes involves a co-author outside the credited names, and a citation that claims it would invite the very attribution dispute he wants to avoid. I also take his point on B002. A two-name Kiyotaki-Moore pair is a cleaner alternative than the ballot's four-name entry, and I would back that version if the Committee turned to B002. Where I would press him is on what the narrow unit implies for confidence. A narrow unit makes the sensitivity question easier to test, so I would want the Committee to say openly that this part of the case rests on background knowledge.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B013 first. She argues that the task framework with Katz-Murphy relative-supply logic provides the conceptual account and the China-shock designs provide transparent identification. She keeps Katz over Dorn and accepts that Autor, Hanson and Dorn is a defensible alternative trio. She also says B001 is the strongest alternative and that counts do not measure merit.
responses.response: I agree that counts do not measure merit and that I do not rely on them. Her case for B013 is the strongest of the alternatives. I stay at B001 for three reasons. The remaining dispute in B013 is empirical (magnitude and persistence of the local effects), where for B001 it is mostly about implementation. The credit in B013 splits across two strands, and I cannot find a rule that decides between Katz and Dorn without a judgement the evidence does not settle. And the framework overlaps with recent recognition of work on technology and institutions. I still hold B013 as my first alternative. If the Committee moved to B013, I would favour defining the citation by the wage-structure and trade-exposure evidence, as she suggests. I would give the third slot to whichever of Katz or Dorn the Committee judges more central to that defined achievement, and I do not think I can settle that choice alone.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B050 first with Melitz and Helpman. He treats Melitz (2003) as the origin and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple as constitutive. He accepts that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum and Redding are a real attribution cost, and he now treats B001 as a close alternative. He says he would not move B001 ahead of B050 on support counts alone.
responses.response: I agree that support counts should not decide this, and I did not use them as evidence of merit. His own account of the attribution cost is what keeps B050 behind B001 for me. Parallel contributors sit outside the ballot entry, and he concedes the quantitative gains depend on model specification, while the qualitative selection margins are better supported. A tight Melitz and Helpman citation would be coherent and I would not regard it as a poor outcome. I would ask the Committee to compare how far each candidate's central claims have been checked, not how well each is known. On that criterion BLP-type methods have had more direct stress-testing. I am also persuaded that the Helpman credit in B021 can be kept out of a firm-heterogeneity citation, so that is not my reason for ranking B050 lower.

uncertainties: Whether the third slot should go to Levinsohn (method-level citation) or Bresnahan (programme-level citation). I would not treat either as a scientific error, and the Committee has not settled it.

Whether the Committee treats a measurement toolkit as a discovery. I answer yes if it created new counterfactuals and changed practice, but members who weigh the two differently could reasonably disagree.

How often the documented numerical, instrument and functional-form sensitivities reverse a merger-review or welfare conclusion in practice. A systematic reanalysis or many-analyst test on the same market data would change my confidence, and I have not seen one in the supplied evidence.
How much of Pakes's dynamic-games and production-function work the citation should claim without crediting co-authors outside the three names.
Whether a second achievement could be added within the cap without weakening the citation. I see no pairing that keeps the credit as clean as the single part, so I do not propose one.
My adoption, sensitivity and citation claims rest on background knowledge and on colleagues' round 1 statements, and I have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to any credited name on B001, B013, B002 or my named alternatives is apparent from the supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Johannesson) and the Harvard evolutionary-dynamics network (Rand, Fudenberg, Nowak) are not credited on any of them. My collaboration with Abel Brodeur's Institute for Replication does not involve a candidate. I co-authored with Tore Ellingsen in 2009 and with Johan Almenberg in 2015, and neither is a candidate. I have no co-authorship with the colleagues whose positions I discuss above, as far as the profile shows. My metascience orientation shapes how heavily I weigh stress-testing and robustness. It is a perspective on the evidence and not a personal connection. These are disclosed, not adjudicated.
